clue.text: World of possibility unknown in nurse short of capital

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within the other
a capital is a leading letter, so being short of it means the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: to foster is to nurse or bring up
Y is one of the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: A nurse, short of money, wonders what possibilities remain unknown to her.
explanation.walkthrough: FOSTER drops its capital F to leave OSTER, and the unknown Y goes inside to make OYSTER.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'the world is your oyster' means every opportunity lies open, so the shellfish stands for a world of possibility.

clue.text: It’s done now, having been worked out

definitions.text: It’s done now, having been worked out

indicators.note: something worked out has been processed and reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sigh of relief that a task is finished now it has been solved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is this clue itself: once solved, the solver has 'one down', the first clue in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Solving this clue completes one entry, and 1-down is also its own position in the grid.

clue.text: Asian capital someone discussed?

indicators.note: something discussed is spoken about, so the word is judged by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: a soul is a person, as in 'not a soul'

explanation.surface: A capital city in Asia being mentioned in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: A soul means someone in phrases like 'not a living soul'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seoul is the capital city of South Korea, in East Asia.

clue.text: Dead nice, oddly, poking something akin to a dead parrot?

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so alternate letters are kept
to poke is to push into a thing, so one piece goes inside the second

blocks.clueFragment: something akin to a dead parrot
blocks.note: Monty Python's dead parrot is an 'ex-parrot', and a tit is another bird, so a dead one is an ex-tit

explanation.surface: A gloomy joke about a dead parrot that is oddly rather nice.
explanation.walkthrough: In Monty Python's famous comedy sketch a customer complains that his parrot is dead: 'This is an ex-parrot!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Extinct means no longer living, a species wiped out, so it is a fair synonym for dead.

clue.text: Spice girl on the ball

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing placed on another follows it, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: a nut is slang for a testicle, a ball

explanation.surface: A Spice Girl showing her skill with a football.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the pop group the Spice Girls and a footballer; 'Spice' is the definition and the girl sits after the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutmeg is the hard aromatic seed grated as a kitchen spice.

clue.text: Sent up, quote on sporting union – leaked?

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing on another sits above it, so the pieces stack together
sending something up in a down answer makes it read from the bottom upwards

explanation.surface: A sports union's quote has been leaked to the press and sent up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaked' reads as a news story getting out, but it is slang for urinating; the question mark flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Uretic means relating to urine, and to take a leak is British slang for urinating.

clue.text: Fed narcotics originally, rum I claimed – having similar effect?

indicators.note: the origin is the start, so only the first letter is kept
rum means strange or odd, so the letters come out in an odd order
something fed is put into another thing, so one piece goes inside

explanation.surface: Someone admits a fondness for rum after being fed drugs, claiming it works the same way.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the rest of the clue: something with an effect similar to narcotics.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcotics are drugs, and something medicinal acts like a drug on the body, so its effect is similar.

clue.text: Case against thug in fancy dress?

indicators.note: against means beside or next to, so the pieces are placed together

blocks.note: a gorilla is slang for a brutish thug
a suit is a legal case

explanation.surface: A court case brought against a thug who turned up in costume.
explanation.walkthrough: The case is a lawsuit, placed after the thug although the clue mentions it first.
explanation.definitionFit: A gorilla suit is a classic hairy costume worn to fancy-dress parties.

clue.text: Spat with in-laws to put right, day breaking – what then?

indicators.note: putting something right means sorting and rearranging it, so the letters are reordered
breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: After a quarrel with the in-laws, how do you settle it at daybreak?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the question: after a spat at break of day, what comes next? A duel. 'Day breaking' suggests dawn, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Pistols at dawn was the traditional duel used to settle a quarrel of honour, the escalation that follows a spat.

clue.text: Australian’s arrested on backing loser

indicators.note: to arrest is to take hold of, so one piece holds the other inside it
going backwards means the letters run from right to left

blocks.note: Oz is the informal name for Australia

explanation.surface: An Australian has been arrested for betting on a losing horse.
explanation.walkthrough: OZ holds RE to make OREZ, which is then read backwards. The 's is 'has', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A zero is a nobody, a person of no account, which is the slang sense of a loser.

clue.text: Trouble entering bids, those finally going in

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: tenders are formal bids for a contract

explanation.surface: Trouble breaks out over bids, with the last ones finally submitted.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the tail is the weakest batsmen at the end of the order; 'going in' means going in to bat, not entering a building.
explanation.definitionFit: Tail-enders are the lower-order batsmen in cricket, the last players of a side who come out to bat.

clue.text: Pooka chowin’ down in the audience?

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: gobbling is eating greedily, chowing down, with the dropped g mirrored in the clue

explanation.surface: A sprite in a theatre crowd munching snacks during the show.
explanation.walkthrough: A pooka is a mischievous spirit of Irish folklore. The apostrophe in 'chowin'' signals the clipped pronunciation the sound-alike needs.
explanation.definitionFit: The pooka is a shape-shifting Irish sprite, so a mischievous goblin is a fair general term for it.

clue.text: Fool in cult, or out

indicators.note: something out is put out of place or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A foolish person who is either a member of a cult or has left it.
explanation.walkthrough: Trinculo is the jester in Shakespeare's The Tempest. 'Fool' reads as a common insult but names a stage clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Trinculo is the court jester of Shakespeare's The Tempest, a professional fool in the theatrical sense.

clue.text: Voguish, cooler hat for a baby

blocks.note: a fan is a device that cools
tile is old slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Recommending a trendy sun hat to keep a baby cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like an adjective comparing hats, but it is a noun: a thing that cools.
explanation.definitionFit: Infantile describes anything relating to or suited to infants, the earliest stage of childhood.

clue.text: Quite slow, though not cricket?

blocks.note: second meaning: unfair, more than one should have to put up with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not cricket' is a British idiom for unfair behaviour; the surface pretends to describe a slow game that is not cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means rather dim-witted, and in British idiom it also means unreasonable or unfair, as conduct that breaks the spirit of sport.

clue.text: Empire builder where 2 is, with 25 at the 25, say?

indicators.note: to say something is to speak it, so the result is judged by sound

blocks.note: Seoul (2) is in Korea; tack REAR (25) on the rear of the four letters and they sound like that phrase

explanation.surface: A puzzling riddle asking where an empire builder belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross-references: 2 is SEOUL, which is in Korea, and 25 is REAR. The four letters followed by REAR sound roughly like 'in Korea', said without a final r.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas built a vast Andean empire in South America before the Spanish conquest.

clue.text: See 7 Down
Drive a coach that’s emptied – then leaves

indicators.note: something emptied has lost its contents, leaving just its outside letters

blocks.note: a spin is a drive in a car
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A coach empties of passengers, who then leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as a verb for departing passengers but is a noun for a leafy vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinach is a vegetable eaten for its dark green edible foliage.

clue.text: Couple on trail of solitary tree, perennial also able to survive wintry conditions

definitions.text: Couple on trail of solitary tree

blocks.note: the laurel is an evergreen perennial shrub

explanation.surface: A gardener's description of hardy perennials along a woodland path.
explanation.walkthrough: The comedy duo sang 'The Trail of the Lonesome Pine' in their film Way Out West, so the definition is a coded song title.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy were the comic double act famous for performing 'On the Trail of the Lonesome Pine'.

clue.text: Public school short of an emergency room for Eurasian native

indicators.note: to be short of something is to lack it, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: Roedean is an English girls' boarding school near Brighton
the usual abbreviation for an emergency room

explanation.surface: A private school lacking a sick bay for a pupil from Eurasia.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is a private fee-paying one. 'Native' reads as a person but is an animal native to the region.
explanation.definitionFit: The roe deer is a small deer whose natural range spans Europe and much of Asia.

clue.text: Describe vermin in trap having lifted lid

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the lid is the top, and lifting it off in a down answer removes the first letter

explanation.surface: Recounting how a rat got into a trap after its lid was lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer the lid is the top letter, so lifting it off removes the first letter of the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrate is to tell a story or give an account, which is a sense of describe.

clue.text: Sweet VIPs on the rise

indicators.note: rising in a down answer means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: nobs are important people, and the plural gives two of them

explanation.surface: Pleasant news that very important people are gaining in status.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural VIPs supplies two nobs, which rise together.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonbon is a small piece of confectionery, a type of sweet.

clue.text: Reversing, run free over old, unpaved track

indicators.note: to be over something is to cover it, so one piece wraps the other
going in reverse means the letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: A car backing up and running freely over an old, rough track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversing' at the start applies to everything that follows, not just the first word; the whole assembled string is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirt road has a surface of bare earth, with no tarmac or paving on it.

clue.text: Prompt review of other banking times

indicators.note: a review revises and reworks material, so the letters are rearranged
banking means depositing for safekeeping, so one piece is held within the second

explanation.surface: A quick look over the accounts of other banks at various times.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters hold X between their first and second letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhort is to urge someone strongly to act, which is the verb sense of prompt.

clue.text: See 17 Across
Pop star sees passionate violin player in decline

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to die is to decline, fade away
the bow is what plays a violin's strings

explanation.surface: A pop star watches a passionate violinist whose career is fading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Violin player' suggests a person, but it is the bow drawn across the strings.
explanation.definitionFit: David Bowie was the hugely successful English rock and pop singer behind Ziggy Stardust.

clue.text: Lift up buttocks

blocks.note: first meaning: raise upright, as a horse does

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like an exercise instruction; the two halves are separate meanings, one a verb and one a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for raising something upright and as a noun for a person's bottom.

clue.text: Good day, man, for outdoor pursuit

blocks.note: a king is a chess man

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting to a fellow walker on a country trail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a piece in chess, of which the king is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiking is long-distance walking in the countryside, a popular open-air recreation.

clue.text: Not all there, unlikely granny will return diamond

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is present, so the letters sit inside other words
returning means coming back the other way, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: A confused old lady is unlikely to give back a diamond ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not all there' suggests a muddled granny, but it says only part of the words is used. The definition is loose: argyle is a diamond pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyle is a knitting pattern of interlocking diamond shapes, seen on Scottish socks and jumpers.
